From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Forming something new and somehow valuable

For other uses, see [Creativity (disambiguation)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Creativity_(disambiguation) "Creativity (disambiguation)").

[![graphic of a lightbulb](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3c/Crystal_Clear_app_ktip.svg/250px-Crystal_Clear_app_ktip.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Crystal_Clear_app_ktip.svg)

A picture of an [incandescent light bulb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Incandescent_light_bulb "Incandescent light bulb"), a symbol associated with the formation of an [idea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Idea "Idea"), an example of creativity

**Creativity** is the ability to generate novel and valuable [ideas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Idea "Idea") or works through the exercise of [imagination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imagination "Imagination"). The products of creativity may be classified as either intangible or physical. Intangible products of creativity include ideas, [scientific theories](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scientific_theories "Scientific theories"), [literary works](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Literary_work "Literary work"), [musical compositions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musical_composition "Musical composition"), and [jokes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joke "Joke"). Physical products of creativity include [inventions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Invention "Invention"), dishes or meals, pieces of [jewelry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jewelry "Jewelry"), [costumes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costume "Costume"), and [paintings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Painting "Painting").

Creativity may also describe the ability to find [new solutions to problems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Creative_problem-solving "Creative problem-solving") or new methods to accomplish a goal. Therefore, creativity enables people to [solve problems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solves_problem "Solves problem") in new ways.

Most ancient cultures (including [ancient Greece](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Greece "Ancient Greece"), [ancient China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_China#Ancient_China "History of China"), and [ancient India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outline_of_ancient_India "Outline of ancient India")) lacked the concept of creativity, seeing art as a form of [discovery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_(observation) "Discovery (observation)") rather than a form of creation. In the [Judeo-Christian-Islamic tradition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judeo-Christian_tradition "Judeo-Christian tradition"), creativity is seen as the sole province of God, and human creativity was considered an expression of God's work; the modern conception of creativity came about during the [Renaissance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renaissance "Renaissance"), influenced by [humanist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humanism "Humanism") ideas.[*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*][*[clarification needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Please_clarify "Wikipedia:Please clarify")*]

Scholarly interest in creativity is found in several disciplines, primarily [psychology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychology "Psychology"), [business studies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Business_studies "Business studies"), and [cognitive science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cognitive_science "Cognitive science"). It is also present in education and the [humanities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humanities "Humanities") (including [philosophy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philosophy "Philosophy") and [the arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_arts "The arts")).

## Etymology

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Creativity&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Etymology")]

The English word "creativity" comes from the [Latin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin "Latin") term *creare* (meaning "to create"). Its [derivational suffixes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morphological_derivation "Morphological derivation") also come from Latin, such as the etymological root “crescere”, which means “to let things grow”. This aspect of creativity is emphasized more in indigenous and Eastern concepts of creativity.[*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*] The word "create" appeared in English as early as the 14th century—notably in Chaucer's [The Parson's Tale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Parson's_Tale "The Parson's Tale")[[1]](#cite_note-:18-1) to indicate divine creation.[[2]](#cite_note-RuncoAlbert-2) The modern meaning of creativity in reference to human creation did not emerge until after the [Age of Enlightenment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Age_of_Enlightenment "Age of Enlightenment").[*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]

## Definition

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Creativity&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Definition")]

In a summary of scientific research into creativity, psychology professor Michael Mumford wrote, "We seem to have reached a general agreement that creativity involves the production of [novel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Originality "Originality"), useful products."[[3]](#cite_note-3) Similarly, in psychologist [Robert Sternberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Sternberg "Robert Sternberg")'s words, creativity produces "something original and worthwhile".[[4]](#cite_note-Sternberg_Cognitive_Psychology_2011-4)

Authors have diverged dramatically in their precise definitions beyond these general commonalities: social geographer Peter Meusburger estimated that over a hundred different definitions can be found in the literature.[[5]](#cite_note-Meusburger1-5) One definition given by [Dr. E. Paul Torrance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ellis_Paul_Torrance "Ellis Paul Torrance") in the context of assessing an individual's creative ability is "a process of becoming sensitive to problems, deficiencies, gaps in knowledge, missing elements, disharmonies; identifying the difficulty; searching for solutions, making guesses, or formulating hypotheses about the deficiencies: testing and retesting these hypotheses and possibly modifying and retesting them; and finally communicating the results."[[6]](#cite_note-Torrance_Test_Manual_Verbal-6)

Philosophy professor Ignacio L. Götz, following the etymology of the word, argued that creativity is not necessarily "making". He confined it to the act of creating without thinking about the end product.[[7]](#cite_note-:16-7) While many definitions of creativity seem almost synonymous with originality, Götz also emphasized the difference between creativity and originality. Götz asserted that one can be creative without necessarily being original. When someone creates something, they are certainly creative at that point, but they may not be original in the sense that their creation is not something new.[[7]](#cite_note-:16-7)

Creativity in general is usually distinguished from [innovation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Innovation "Innovation") in particular, where the emphasis is on implementation. Academics and authors [Teresa Amabile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teresa_Amabile "Teresa Amabile") and Michael Pratt defined creativity as the production of novel and useful ideas and innovation as the implementation of creative ideas,[[8]](#cite_note-8) while the [OECD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OECD "OECD") and [Eurostat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eurostat "Eurostat") stated that "innovation is more than a new idea or an invention; an innovation requires implementation, either by being put into active use or by being made available for use by other parties, firms, individuals, or organizations."[[9]](#cite_note-9)[[10]](#cite_note-10)

There is also emotional creativity,[[11]](#cite_note-11) which is described as a pattern of cognitive abilities and personality traits related to originality and appropriateness in emotional experience.[[12]](#cite_note-12)

From an interdisciplinary point a view, creativity can serve to increase neuronal connectivity, cognitive and emotional coherence as well as social cohesion.[[13]](#cite_note-13) In this respect, creativity can help to cope with despair, hate and violence.[[14]](#cite_note-14)

## Conceptual history

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Creativity&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Conceptual history")]

Main article: [History of the concept of creativity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_concept_of_creativity "History of the concept of creativity")

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/4/4a/Plato-raphael.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Plato-raphael.jpg)

Greek philosophers like Plato rejected the concept of creativity, preferring to see art as a form of discovery. When asked in *[The Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_(Plato) "Republic (Plato)")*, "Will we say, of a painter, that he makes something?", Plato answers, "Certainly not, he merely [imitates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mimesis "Mimesis")."[[15]](#cite_note-SixIdeas-15)

### Ancient

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Creativity&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Ancient")]

Most ancient cultures, including [ancient Greece](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Greece "Ancient Greece"),[[15]](#cite_note-SixIdeas-15) [ancient China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_China#Ancient_China "History of China"), and [ancient India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outline_of_ancient_India "Outline of ancient India"),[[16]](#cite_note-Albert99-16) lacked the concept of creativity, seeing art as a form of discovery and not creation. The ancient Greeks had no terms for "to create" or "creator" except for the expression *poiein* (to make), which only applied to *poiesis* (poetry) and to the *poietes* (poet, or "maker", who made it). [Plato](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plato "Plato") did not believe in art as a form of creation. He asks in the *[Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_(Plato) "Republic (Plato)")*,[[17]](#cite_note-17) "Will we say of a painter that he makes something?" He answers, "Certainly not, he merely [imitates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mimesis "Mimesis")."[[15]](#cite_note-SixIdeas-15)

It is commonly argued that the notion of "creativity" originated in [Western cultures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_culture "Western culture") through Christianity, as a matter of [divine inspiration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Revelation "Revelation").[[2]](#cite_note-RuncoAlbert-2) According to scholars, the earliest Western conception of creativity was the [Biblical story of the creation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genesis_creation_narrative "Genesis creation narrative") given in *[Genesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Book_of_Genesis "Book of Genesis")*.[[16]](#cite_note-Albert99-16): 18 However, this is not creativity in the modern sense, which did not arise until the [Renaissance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renaissance "Renaissance"). In the Judeo-Christian-Islamic tradition, creativity was the sole province of God; humans were not considered to have the ability to create something new except as an expression of God's work.[[18]](#cite_note-NiuSternberg-18) A similar concept existed in Greek culture, where the [Muses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muse "Muse") were seen as mediating inspiration from the gods.[[19]](#cite_note-Dacey-19) Romans and Greeks invoked the concept of an external creative "[daemon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daemon_(classical_mythology) "Daemon (classical mythology)")" (Greek) or "[genius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genius_(mythology) "Genius (mythology)")" (Latin), linked to the sacred or the divine. However, none of these views are similar to the modern concept of creativity, and the rejection of creativity in favor of discovery and the belief that individual creation was a conduit of the divine would dominate the West until the Renaissance and even later.[[18]](#cite_note-NiuSternberg-18)[[16]](#cite_note-Albert99-16): 18–19

### Renaissance

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Creativity&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Renaissance")]

It was during the Renaissance that creativity was first conceived not as a conduit from the divine, but as arising from the abilities of "[great men](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Man_theory "Great Man theory")".[[16]](#cite_note-Albert99-16): 18–19 This could be attributed to the leading intellectual movement of the time, aptly named [humanism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humanism "Humanism"), which developed an intensely anthropocentric outlook on the world, valuing the intellect and achievement of the individual.[[20]](#cite_note-20) From this philosophy arose the [Renaissance man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renaissance_man "Renaissance man") (or polymath), an individual who embodies the principles of humanism in their ceaseless courtship with knowledge and creation.[[21]](#cite_note-21) One of the most well-known and immensely accomplished examples is [Leonardo da Vinci](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonardo_da_Vinci "Leonardo da Vinci").

### From the 17th to the 19th centuries

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Creativity&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: From the 17th to the 19th centuries")]

However, the shift from divine inspiration to the abilities of the individual was gradual and would not become immediately apparent until the [Age of Enlightenment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Age_of_Enlightenment "Age of Enlightenment").[[16]](#cite_note-Albert99-16): 19–21 By the 18th century, creativity (notably in [aesthetics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aesthetics "Aesthetics")) linked with the concept of imagination became more frequent.[[15]](#cite_note-SixIdeas-15) In the writing of [Thomas Hobbes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Hobbes "Thomas Hobbes"), imagination became a key element of human cognition.[[2]](#cite_note-RuncoAlbert-2) [William Duff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Duff_(writer) "William Duff (writer)") was one of the first to identify imagination as a quality of genius, typifying the separation being made between talent (productive, but not breaking new ground) and genius.[[19]](#cite_note-Dacey-19)

As an independent topic of study, creativity received little attention until the 19th century.[[19]](#cite_note-Dacey-19) Psychologist Mark Runco and Robert Albert argue that creativity as the subject of proper study began seriously to emerge in the late 19th century with the increased interest in individual differences inspired by the arrival of [Darwinism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Darwinism "Darwinism"). In particular, they refer to the work of [Francis Galton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_Galton "Francis Galton"), who, through his [eugenicist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eugenics "Eugenics") outlook, took a keen interest in the heritability of intelligence, with creativity taken as an aspect of genius.[[2]](#cite_note-RuncoAlbert-2)

### Modern

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Creativity&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Modern")]

In the late 19th and early 20th centuries, leading mathematicians and scientists such as [Hermann von Helmholtz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermann_von_Helmholtz "Hermann von Helmholtz") (1896)[[22]](#cite_note-22) and [Henri Poincaré](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henri_Poincaré "Henri Poincaré") (1908)[[23]](#cite_note-23) began to reflect on and publicly discuss their creative processes. The insights of Poincaré and von Helmholtz inspired the accounts of the creative process by pioneering theorists such as [Graham Wallas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graham_Wallas "Graham Wallas") and [Max Wertheimer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_Wertheimer "Max Wertheimer"). In his work *Art of Thought*, published in 1926,[[24]](#cite_note-Wallas26-24) Wallas presented one of the first models of the creative process. In the Wallas model, creative insights and illuminations may be explained by a process consisting of five stages:

1. *preparation* (preparatory work on a problem that focuses the individual's mind on the problem and explores the problem's dimensions),
2. *[incubation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Incubation_(psychology) "Incubation (psychology)")* (in which the problem is internalized into the unconscious mind although nothing appears externally to be happening),
3. *intimation* (the creative person gets a "feeling" that a solution is on its way),
4. *illumination* or insight (in which the creative idea bursts forth from its [preconscious](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Preconscious "Preconscious") processing into conscious awareness);
5. *verification* (in which the idea is consciously verified, elaborated, and then applied).

Wallas's model is also often treated as four stages, with "intimation" seen as a sub-stage.

Wallas considered creativity to be a legacy of the [evolutionary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evolution "Evolution") process, which allowed humans to quickly adapt to rapidly changing environments. Simonton[[25]](#cite_note-Simonton99-25) provides an updated perspective on this view in his book, *Origins of Genius: Darwinian Perspectives on Creativity*.

In 1927, mathematician and philosopher [Alfred North Whitehead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_North_Whitehead "Alfred North Whitehead") gave the Gifford Lectures at the [University of Edinburgh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Edinburgh "University of Edinburgh"), later published as *[Process and Reality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Process_and_Reality "Process and Reality")*.[[26]](#cite_note-26) He is credited with having coined the term "creativity" to serve as the ultimate category of his metaphysical scheme.[[27]](#cite_note-27)

Although psychometric studies of creativity had been conducted by The London School of Psychology as early as 1927 with the work of H.L. Hargreaves into the Faculty of Imagination.[[28]](#cite_note-28) The formal [psychometric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychometrics "Psychometrics") measurement of creativity, from the standpoint of orthodox [psychological](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychology "Psychology") literature, is usually considered to have begun with psychologist [J.P. Guilford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J.P._Guilford "J.P. Guilford")'s address to the [American Psychological Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Psychological_Association "American Psychological Association") in 1950.[[29]](#cite_note-Sternberg99-29) That address helped to popularize the study of creativity and to focus attention on scientific approaches to conceptualizing creativity. Statistical analyzes led to the recognition of creativity as an aspect of human cognition separate from [IQ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intelligence_quotient "Intelligence quotient")-type intelligence, under the study of which it had previously been subsumed. Guilford's work suggested that above a threshold level of IQ, the relationship between creativity and classically measured intelligence broke down.[[30]](#cite_note-Kozbelt-30)

### Across cultures

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Creativity&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Across cultures")]

Creativity is viewed differently in different countries.[[31]](#cite_note-31) For example, cross-cultural research centered in Hong Kong found that Westerners view creativity more in terms of the individual attributes of a person, such as their aesthetic taste, while Chinese people view creativity more in terms of the social influence of creative people (i.e. what they can contribute to society).[[32]](#cite_note-32) Mpofu, et al., surveyed 28 African languages and found that 27 had no word which directly translated to "creativity", with Arabic being the exception.[[33]](#cite_note-Mpofu-33): 465 The [linguistic relativity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linguistic_relativity "Linguistic relativity") hypothesis (i.e. that language can affect thought) suggests that the lack of an equivalent word for "creativity" may affect the views of creativity among speakers of such languages. However, more research would be needed to establish this, and there is certainly no suggestion that this linguistic difference makes people any less—or more—creative. Nevertheless, it is true that there has been very little research on creativity in Africa[[33]](#cite_note-Mpofu-33): 458 and Latin America.[[34]](#cite_note-34) Creativity has been more thoroughly researched in the northern hemisphere, but there are cultural differences between northern countries. In Scandinavia, creativity is seen as an individual attitude that helps people cope with life's challenges,[[35]](#cite_note-35) while in Germany, creativity is seen more as a process that can be applied to help solve problems.[[36]](#cite_note-36)

## Classification

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Creativity&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Classification")]

### "Four C" model

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Creativity&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: ")]

Psychologists [James Kaufman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_C._Kaufman "James C. Kaufman") and Ronald Beghetto introduced a "four C" model of creativity. The four "C's" are:

1. *mini-c* ("transformative learning" involving "personally meaningful interpretations of experiences, actions, and insights").
2. *little-c* (everyday problem-solving and creative expression).
3. *Pro-C* (exhibited by people who are professionally or vocationally creative, though not necessarily eminent).
4. *Big-C* (creativity considered great in a given field).

This model was intended to help accommodate models and theories of creativity that stressed competence as an essential component and a historic transformation of a creative domain as the highest mark of creativity. It also, the authors argued, made a useful framework for analyzing creative processes in individuals.[[37]](#cite_note-KaufBeg2009-37)

The contrast signified by the terms "Big C" and "little C" has been widely used. Kozbelt, Beghetto, and Runco used a little-c/Big-C model to review major theories of creativity.[[30]](#cite_note-Kozbelt-30) [Margaret Boden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Boden "Margaret Boden") distinguished between h-creativity (historical) and p-creativity (personal).[[38]](#cite_note-Boden2004-38)

[Ken Robinson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ken_Robinson_(educationalist) "Ken Robinson (educationalist)")[[39]](#cite_note-allourfutures-39) and Anna Craft[[40]](#cite_note-Craft1-40) focused on creativity in a general population, particularly with respect to education. Craft makes a similar distinction between "high" and "little c" creativity[[40]](#cite_note-Craft1-40) and cites Robinson as referring to "high" and "democratic" creativity. [Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mihaly_Csikszentmihalyi "Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi") defined creativity in terms of individuals judged to have made significant creative and perhaps domain-changing contributions.[[41]](#cite_note-Csik1-41) Simonton analyzed the career trajectories of eminent creative people in order to map patterns and predictors of creative productivity.[[42]](#cite_note-Simonton97-42)

### "Four P's" aspects

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Creativity&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: ")]

Theories of creativity (and empirical investigations of why some people are more creative than others) have focused on a variety of aspects. The dominant factors are usually identified as "the four P's," a framework first put forward by [Mel Rhodes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Melvin_Rhodes "James Melvin Rhodes"):[[43]](#cite_note-43)

Process
:   A focus on *process* is shown in cognitive approaches that try to describe thought mechanisms and techniques for creative thinking. Theories invoking [divergent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divergent_thinking "Divergent thinking") rather than [convergent thinking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convergent_thinking "Convergent thinking") (such as that of [Guilford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._P._Guilford "J. P. Guilford")), or those describing the staging of the creative process (such as that of [Wallas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graham_Wallas "Graham Wallas")) are primarily theories of the creative process.

Product
:   A focus on a creative *product* usually attempts to assess creative output, whether for psychometrics (see below) or to understand why some objects are considered creative. It is from a consideration of product that the standard definition of creativity as the production of something both novel and useful arises.[[44]](#cite_note-44)

Person
:   A focus on the nature of the creative *person* considers more general intellectual habits, such as openness, levels of [ideation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ideation_(creative_process) "Ideation (creative process)"), autonomy, expertise, exploratory behavior, and so on.

Press and place
:   A focus on *place* (or *press*) considers the circumstances in which creativity flourishes, such as degrees of autonomy, access to resources, and the nature of gatekeepers. Creative lifestyles are characterized by nonconforming attitudes and behaviors, as well as flexibility.[[45]](#cite_note-Sternberg_2009_468-45)

### "Five A's" aspects

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Creativity&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: ")]

In 2013, based on a sociocultural critique of the Four-P's model as individualistic, static, and decontextualized, psychology professor and author Vlad Petre Glăveanu proposed a "Five A's" model consisting of actor, action, artifact, audience, and affordance.[[46]](#cite_note-46) In this model, the *actor* is the person with attributes but who is also located within social networks; *action* is the process of creativity not only in internal cognitive terms but also external, bridging the gap between [ideation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ideation_(creative_process) "Ideation (creative process)") and implementation; *artifacts* emphasize how creative products typically represent cumulative innovations over time rather than abrupt discontinuities; and "press/place" is divided into *audience* and *affordance*, which consider the interdependence of the creative individual with the social and material world, respectively. Although not supplanting the Four P's model in creativity research, the Five A's model has exerted influence over the direction of some creativity research,[[47]](#cite_note-Mattson_et_al_2021-47) and has been credited with bringing coherence to studies across a number of creative domains.[[48]](#cite_note-Sun_&_Okada_2021-48)

## Process theories

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Creativity&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Process theories")]

There has been significant research conducted in the fields of [psychology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychology "Psychology") and [cognitive science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cognitive_science "Cognitive science") towards better understanding the processes by which creativity occurs. The results of these studies have led to several possible explanations of the sources and methods of creativity.[[1]](#cite_note-:18-1)

### Incubation

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Creativity&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Incubation")]

Main article: [Incubation (psychology)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Incubation_(psychology) "Incubation (psychology)")

"Incubation" is a temporary break from [creative problem solving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Creative_problem_solving "Creative problem solving") that can result in insight.[[49]](#cite_note-EoC_Incubation-49) Empirical research has investigated whether, as the concept of "incubation" in [Wallas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graham_Wallas "Graham Wallas")'s model implies, a period of interruption or rest from a problem may aid creative problem-solving. Early work proposed that creative solutions to problems arise mysteriously from the unconscious mind while the conscious mind is occupied with other tasks.[[50]](#cite_note-Anderson2000-50) This hypothesis is included in [Csikszentmihalyi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mihaly_Csikszentmihalyi "Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi")'s five-phase model of the creative process, which describes incubation as a time when one's unconscious takes over. This was supposed to allow for unique connections to be made without the conscious mind trying to make logical order out of the problem.[[51]](#cite_note-51)

Ward[[52]](#cite_note-Ward2003-52) listed various hypotheses that have been advanced to explain why incubation may aid creative problem-solving and notes how some [empirical evidence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Empirical_evidence "Empirical evidence") is consistent with a different hypothesis: incubation aids creative problems in that it enables "forgetting" of misleading clues. The absence of incubation may lead the problem solver to become [fixated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fixation_(psychology) "Fixation (psychology)") on inappropriate problem-solving strategies.[[53]](#cite_note-Smith1995-53)

### Divergent thinking

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Creativity&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Divergent thinking")]

[J. P. Guilford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._P._Guilford "J. P. Guilford")[[54]](#cite_note-Guilford67-54) drew a distinction between convergent and divergent production, or [convergent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convergent_thinking "Convergent thinking") and [divergent thinking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divergent_thinking "Divergent thinking"). Convergent thinking involves aiming for a single, correct, or best solution to a problem (e.g. "How can we get a crewed rocket to land on the moon safely and within budget?"). Divergent thinking, on the other hand, involves the creative generation of multiple answers to an open-ended prompt (e.g. "How can a chair be used?").[[55]](#cite_note-:15-55) Divergent thinking is sometimes used as a synonym for creativity in psychological literature or is considered the necessary precursor to creativity.[[56]](#cite_note-56) However, as Runco pointed out, there is a clear distinction between creative thinking and divergent thinking.[[55]](#cite_note-:15-55) Creative thinking focuses on the production, combination, and assessment of ideas to formulate something new and unique, while divergent thinking focuses on conceiving a variety of ideas that are not necessarily new or unique. Other researchers have occasionally used the terms *flexible* thinking or [fluid intelligence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fluid_and_crystallized_intelligence "Fluid and crystallized intelligence"), which are also roughly similar to (but not synonymous with) creativity.[[57]](#cite_note-57) While convergent and divergent thinking differ greatly in terms of approach to problem solving, it is believed[*[by whom?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual_of_Style/Words_to_watch#Unsupported_attributions "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Words to watch")*] that both are employed to some degree in solving most real-world problems.[[55]](#cite_note-:15-55)

### Geneplore model

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Creativity&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Geneplore model")]

In 1992, Finke, et al., proposed the "Geneplore model", in which creativity takes place in two phases: a generative phase, where an individual constructs mental representations called "preinventive" structures, and an exploratory phase where those structures are used to come up with creative ideas.[[58]](#cite_note-Finke_et_al_1992-58) Some evidence shows that when people use their imagination to develop new ideas, those ideas are structured in predictable ways in accordance with properties of existing categories and concepts.[[59]](#cite_note-Ward1995-59) Weisberg argued, in contrast, that creativity involves ordinary cognitive processes yielding extraordinary results.[[60]](#cite_note-Weisberg93-60)

### Explicit–implicit interaction theory

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Creativity&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Explicit–implicit interaction theory")]

Helie and Sun[[61]](#cite_note-HelieSun2010-61) proposed a framework for understanding [creativity in problem solving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Creative_problem-solving "Creative problem-solving"), namely the explicit–implicit interaction (EII) theory of creativity. This theory attempts to provide a more unified explanation of relevant phenomena (in part by reinterpreting/integrating various fragmentary existing theories of [incubation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Incubation_(psychology) "Incubation (psychology)") and [insight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Insight "Insight")).

The EII theory relies mainly on five basic principles:

1. co-existence of, and the difference between, explicit and implicit knowledge
2. simultaneous involvement of implicit and explicit processes in most tasks
3. redundant representation of explicit and implicit knowledge
4. integration of the results of explicit and implicit processing
5. iterative (and possibly bidirectional) processing

A computational implementation of the theory was developed based on the [CLARION cognitive architecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CLARION_(cognitive_architecture) "CLARION (cognitive architecture)") and used to simulate relevant human data. This work is an initial step in the development of process-based theories of creativity, encompassing incubation, insight, and various other related phenomena.

### Conceptual blending

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Creativity&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Conceptual blending")]

Main article: [Conceptual blending](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conceptual_blending "Conceptual blending")

In *[The Act of Creation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Act_of_Creation "The Act of Creation")*, [Arthur Koestler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Koestler "Arthur Koestler") introduced the concept of "bisociation" – that creativity arises as a result of the intersection of two quite different frames of reference.[[62]](#cite_note-Koestler64-62) In the 1990s, various approaches in cognitive science that dealt with [metaphor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metaphor "Metaphor"), [analogy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Analogy "Analogy"), and structure mapping converged, and a new integrative approach to the study of creativity in science, art, and humor emerged under the label [conceptual blending](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conceptual_blending "Conceptual blending").

### Honing theory

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Creativity&action=edit&section=19 "Edit section: Honing theory")]

Honing theory, developed principally by psychologist [Liane Gabora](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liane_Gabora "Liane Gabora"), posits that creativity arises due to the self-organizing, self-mending nature of a worldview. The creative process is a way by which the individual hones (and re-hones) an integrated worldview. Honing theory places emphasis not only on the externally visible creative outcome but also on the internal cognitive restructuring and repair of the worldview brought about by the creative process.[[63]](#cite_note-:14-63) When one is faced with a creatively demanding task, there is an interaction between one's conception of the task and one's worldview. The conception of the task changes through interaction with the worldview, and the worldview changes through interaction with the task. This interaction is reiterated until the task is complete, at which point the task is conceived of differently and the worldview is subtly or drastically transformed, following the natural tendency of a worldview to attempt to resolve dissonance and seek internal cons

# Creativity – Wikipedia Article Summary

## Overview
Creativity is the ability to generate novel and valuable ideas or works through the exercise of imagination. Products of creativity can be intangible (ideas, scientific theories, literary works, musical compositions, jokes) or physical (inventions, dishes, jewelry, costumes, paintings). Creativity also describes the ability to find new solutions to problems or new methods to accomplish goals.

## Etymology
The English word "creativity" comes from the Latin *creare* ("to create"), with roots in *crescere* ("to let things grow"). The word "create" appeared in English as early as the 14th century (in Chaucer's *The Parson's Tale*) to indicate divine creation. The modern meaning regarding human creation emerged after the Age of Enlightenment.

## Definition
Psychologist Michael Mumford stated: "We seem to have reached a general agreement that creativity involves the production of novel, useful products." Robert Sternberg similarly defines creativity as producing "something original and worthwhile." Over a hundred different definitions exist in the literature. Creativity is generally distinguished from innovation, where innovation emphasizes implementation of creative ideas.

## Conceptual History
- **Ancient**: Most ancient cultures (Greece, China, India) lacked the concept of creativity, viewing art as discovery rather than creation. Plato rejected the idea that painters "make something"—they merely imitate.
- **Judeo-Christian-Islamic tradition**: Creativity was seen as the sole province of God; humans were conduits of divine work.
- **Renaissance**: Creativity was first conceived as arising from the abilities of "great men," influenced by humanism.
- **17th–19th centuries**: The shift from divine inspiration to individual ability was gradual. By the 18th century, creativity became linked with imagination. Francis Galton studied creativity as an aspect of genius through a eugenicist lens.
- **Modern**: Graham Wallas (1926) presented one of the first models of the creative process with five stages: preparation, incubation, intimation, illumination/insight, and verification. Alfred North Whitehead coined the term "creativity" in 1927. J.P. Guilford's 1950 address to the APA popularized the scientific study of creativity, separating it from IQ-type intelligence.

## Classification Models
### Four C Model (Kaufman & Beghetto)
1. **mini-c**: Transformative learning with personally meaningful insights
2. **little-c**: Everyday problem-solving and creative expression
3. **Pro-C**: Professional/vocational creativity (not necessarily eminent)
4. **Big-C**: Creativity considered great in a given field

### Four P's (Mel Rhodes)
- **Process**: Cognitive approaches describing thought mechanisms
- **Product**: Assessing creative output (novel and useful)
- **Person**: Intellectual habits like openness, autonomy, expertise
- **Press/Place**: Circumstances fostering creativity (autonomy, resources, gatekeepers)

### Five A's (Glăveanu, 2013)
A sociocultural model: Actor, Action, Artifact, Audience, Affordance.

## Process Theories
- **Incubation**: A temporary break from creative problem-solving that can result in insight. May help by enabling "forgetting" of misleading clues.
- **Divergent Thinking**: Generating multiple answers to open-ended prompts (distinct from convergent thinking, which aims for a single correct solution).
- **Geneplore Model**: Two phases—generative (constructing "preinventive" structures) and exploratory (using structures for creative ideas).
- **Explicit–Implicit Interaction (EII) Theory**: Creativity involves interaction between explicit and implicit knowledge, with five basic principles.
- **Conceptual Blending**: Arthur Koestler's "bisociation"—creativity arises from intersection of two different frames of reference.
- **Honing Theory**: Creativity arises from self-organizing, self-mending nature of a worldview; internal cognitive restructuring.

## Factors Influencing Creativity
### Intelligence
Five models describe the relationship between creativity and intelligence: creativity as a subset of intelligence, intelligence as a subset of creativity, overlapping yet distinct constructs, coincident sets, and disjoint sets.

### Mental Health
Research has explored connections between creativity and mental health, including bipolar disorders.

### Personal Traits
Includes divergent production, dedication and expertise, and motivation.

### Environment
Circumstances that foster creativity, including degrees of autonomy and access to resources.

## In Different Fields
Creativity is studied across psychology, business studies, cognitive science, education, and the humanities. Research in neuroscience has examined REM sleep and various brain models. Creativity is also studied in economics, sociology, and education (with specific examples from Scotland, China, and the European Union).

## Organizational Creativity
Involves organizational culture, team composition, team processes, and constraints.

## Fostering Creativity
Research includes the concept of "need for closure" and how it affects creativity.

## Malevolent Creativity
Creativity applied to harmful purposes, including crime and predictive factors.

## Academic Journals
Multiple academic journals are dedicated to the study of creativity.

**Creativity** is the [ability](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ability?action=edit&redlink=1 "Ability (not yet started)") to make something new. Creativity is involved in all parts of life - including science, art, writing and music.

Creativity is difficult to [measure](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Measure "Measure"). We do not understand why people are creative. It can be controversial to judge creativity. Some people say that making something is only creative if the thing has never been made before.

Some think that creativity is an important thing that makes [humans](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human "Human") different from [apes](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ape "Ape"). Other people think that apes and other animals use creativity to survive. [Liane Gabora](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liane_Gabora?action=edit&redlink=1 "Liane Gabora (not yet started)") believes that [culture](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Culture "Culture") comes from creativity, it does not come from [imitation](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imitation?action=edit&redlink=1 "Imitation (not yet started)") (copying). Because of this, these people say that [human science](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_science "Human science") should focus on creativity (pay special attention to it). [Ethics](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethics "Ethics") (the study of what is right and wrong) could try to find creative [solutions](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solution "Solution") (fixes) for ethical problems. [Politics](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Politics "Politics") could focus on the [political virtues](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_virtues "Political virtues") that need some creativity. Imitation would not be the focus of [education](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Education "Education"). [Linguistics](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linguistics "Linguistics") might be more interested in how new words are created by culture, rather than in how existing ones are used in [grammar](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammar "Grammar").

[Intellectual interests](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intellectual_interests?action=edit&redlink=1 "Intellectual interests (not yet started)") (recognized as [intellectual rights](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intellectual_rights?action=edit&redlink=1 "Intellectual rights (not yet started)") or [intellectual property](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intellectual_property "Intellectual property") in the [law](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Law "Law")) are a way to [reward](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reward "Reward") creativity in law, but they do not always work very well. A good example is [copyright](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copyright "Copyright") which is supposed to pay [writers](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Writer "Writer") and [artists](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artist "Artist"), but may only pay [lawyers](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawyer "Lawyer") to make (imitative) arguments in [court](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Court "Court").

Creativity is an important idea in [economics](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economics "Economics") (the study of money and businesses), where it is known as **ingenuity** (the ability to come up with new ideas) or **individual capital** - [capacities](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capacity "Capacity") that [individuals](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Individual "Individual") have, that do not arise from simple imitation of what is known already. This is separate from the [instructional capital](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Instructional_capital?action=edit&redlink=1 "Instructional capital (not yet started)") that might try to [capture](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capture?action=edit&redlink=1 "Capture (not yet started)") some of that in a [patent](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patent "Patent") or [training](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Training "Training") system that helps others do what the individual leader or [founder](https://simple.wiktionary.org/wiki/founder "wikt:founder") of the system can do. In [urban economics](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_economics?action=edit&redlink=1 "Urban economics (not yet started)") there are various ways to measure creativity - the [Bohemian Index](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bohemian_Index?action=edit&redlink=1 "Bohemian Index (not yet started)") and [Gay Index](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gay_Index?action=edit&redlink=1 "Gay Index (not yet started)") are two attempts to do this [accurately](https://simple.wiktionary.org/wiki/accurate "wikt:accurate") and [predict](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Predict "Predict") the [economic growth](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_growth "Economic growth") of [cities](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/City "City") based on creativity.

# Using Bloom's Taxonomy to Ask Critical Thinking Questions

October 2016

Audience

Adults

Topic

Standards Aligned

Teaching Techniques

Level

Advanced

Beginning

Intermediate

![Pyramid of Bloom's Taxonomy Labeled from the bottom to the top: Remembering, Understanding, Applying, Analyzing, Evaluating, Creating](/sites/default/files/styles/resource/public/blooms_taxonomy.jpg?itok=yztCvYzR)

“Good learning starts with questions, not answers.” – Guy Claxton

Critical thinking is required in the workplace, in educational settings, and to address everyday challenges. In ESL classes, teachers often ask only factual questions that rely on short-term memory, such as “What did Lee Pa do yesterday?” and “What is the capital of Minnesota?”

While memory is an important skill, teachers should ask questions and plan activities that dig deeper. Even in beginning level classrooms, it is essential that learners are asked questions that challenge them to think critically.

One tool that can be used to incorporate critical thinking questions and activities into the classroom is **Bloom’s Taxonomy**. Bloom’s Taxonomy is a classification system that is used to define and distinguish different levels of human cognition—i.e., thinking, learning, and understanding.

Bloom’s Taxonomy divides thinking into six categories, with one being the simplest level of thinking, up to six, which is the most complex.

1. **Knowledge:** Remembering or recalling appropriate, previously learned information to draw out factual (usually right or wrong) answers. When asking question, use words and phrases such as: how many, when, where, list, define, tell, describe, identify, etc, to draw out factual answers, testing students' recall and recognition.
2. **Comprehension:** Grasping or understanding the meaning of informational materials. When asking question, use words such as: describe, explain, estimate, predict, identify, differentiate, etc, to encourage students to translate, interpret, and extrapolate.
3. **Application:** Applying previously learned information (or knowledge) to new and unfamiliar situations. When asking question, use words such as: demonstrate, apply, illustrate, show, solve, examine, classify, experiment, etc, to encourage students to apply knowledge to situations that are new and unfamiliar.
4. **Analysis:** Breaking down information into parts, or examining (and trying to understand the organizational structure of) information. When asking question, use words and phrases such as: what are the differences, analyze, explain, compare, separate, classify, arrange, etc, to encourage students to break information down into parts.
5. **Synthesis:** Applying prior knowledge and skills to combine elements into a pattern not clearly there before. When asking question, use words and phrases such as: combine, rearrange, substitute, create, design, invent, what if, etc, to encourage students to combine elements into a pattern that's new.
6. **Evaluation:** Judging or deciding according to some set of criteria, without real right or wrong answers. When asking question, use words such as: assess, decide, measure, select, explain, conclude, compare, summarize, etc, to encourage students to make judgements according to a set of criteria.

args.summary:
This webpage from Literacy Minnesota provides guidance on using Bloom's Taxonomy to ask critical thinking questions in ESL (English as a Second Language) classrooms. The resource, published in October 2016, is aimed at adult learners and covers beginning to advanced levels.

Bloom's Taxonomy is presented as a tool for moving beyond simple factual recall questions toward deeper critical thinking. The taxonomy divides thinking into six hierarchical levels:

1. **Knowledge** – Remembering/recalling factual information (question words: how many, when, where, list, define, tell, describe, identify)
2. **Comprehension** – Understanding meaning of information (question words: describe, explain, estimate, predict, identify, differentiate)
3. **Application** – Applying knowledge to new situations (question words: demonstrate, apply, illustrate, show, solve, examine, classify, experiment)
4. **Analysis** – Breaking down information into parts (question words: what are the differences, analyze, explain, compare, separate, classify, arrange)
5. **Synthesis** – Combining elements into new patterns (question words: combine, rearrange, substitute, create, design, invent, what if)
6. **Evaluation** – Making judgments according to criteria (question words: assess, decide, measure, select, explain, conclude, compare, summarize)

The page includes a quote from Guy Claxton: "Good learning starts with questions, not answers." It emphasizes that even in beginning-level classrooms, learners should be challenged to think critically. Links to additional resources on Bloom's Taxonomy question stems and related teaching strategies are provided.

This webpage from Bronx Community College (CUNY) Library's LibGuide explores the relationship between Bloom's Taxonomy and critical thinking, explaining how both are essential for education and metacognition.

**Key Points:**

- Bloom's Taxonomy and critical thinking are closely linked; Bloom's taxonomy guides students through progressive levels of thinking from knowledge/memory to deeper analysis and action.
- The guide covers practical applications including dialogue with texts, teaching extrapolation, and the importance of background knowledge for critical engagement.
- Reasons to use Bloom's Taxonomy include establishing clear learning objectives, helping teachers organize goals, and enabling aligned instruction and assessment.

**The Revised Taxonomy (2001) - Six Cognitive Processes:**
1. Remember (Recognizing, Recalling)
2. Understand (Interpreting, Exemplifying, Classifying, Summarizing, Inferring, Comparing, Explaining)
3. Apply (Executing, Implementing)
4. Analyze (Differentiating, Organizing, Attributing)
5. Evaluate (Checking, Critiquing)
6. Create (Generating, Planning, Producing)

**Four Types of Knowledge in the Revised Taxonomy:**
- Factual Knowledge (terminology, specific details)
- Conceptual Knowledge (classifications, principles, theories)
- Procedural Knowledge (skills, techniques, methods)
- Metacognitive Knowledge (strategic knowledge, self-knowledge)

**Bloom's Original Taxonomy (1956):** Knowledge, Comprehension, Application, Analysis, Synthesis, Evaluation

**Example Application:** A sample using Dr. Martin Luther King Jr.'s "I Have a Dream" speech demonstrates how each level of Bloom's Taxonomy can be applied to a thesis statement, from basic knowledge questions (year of the speech) to evaluation (how would MLK react to current state) and synthesis (constructing an outline of a country without racism).

The guide references sources including Vanderbilt University's Center for Teaching, Anderson et al.'s 2001 revision of Bloom's Taxonomy, and a 2020 article by Michele De Gastyne.

# How to Use Bloom's Taxonomy in Lessons

In this blog post, we are diving into the concept of Bloom's Taxonomy, a fundamental framework in education that helps teachers develop effective learning objectives and assess student progress. Understanding Bloom's Taxonomy is crucial for educators at every level, as it breaks down the cognitive processes involved in learning, guiding teachers in moving students from basic recall to higher-order critical thinking skills.

Bloom’s Taxonomy is commonly visualized as a pyramid with six levels: Remember, Understand, Apply, Analyze, Evaluate, and Create. As educators, we aim to move students up this pyramid to foster critical thinking. However, it’s essential to acknowledge that the lower levels—Remembering and Understanding—are just as vital, especially when introducing new concepts.

### Breaking Down Bloom's Taxonomy:

1. **Remember**: At the foundation, students must first recall or identify facts. This is a crucial step when starting new lessons. For example, in an elementary classroom, you might have students identify the main idea in a story or list the stages of mitosis in high school biology.
2. **Understand**: After remembering, students need to demonstrate comprehension. This could involve summarizing key details from a reading passage or explaining a scientific concept such as mitosis.
3. **Apply**: Students take what they know and apply it to new situations. For instance, in middle school math, students may solve real-world problems by applying their understanding of ratios and proportional relationships.
4. **Analyze**: This level involves breaking down information into parts and examining relationships. In a math class, students might analyze multi-step problems by comparing proportional relationships, identifying patterns, or recognizing trends.
5. **Evaluate**: At this stage, students critically assess information. In a biology class, for example, students could evaluate the consequences of errors in cell division by reading case studies and analyzing their impact on health.
6. **Create**: The highest level, where students synthesize information to generate new ideas. This could involve designing their own experiments in a science class or creating a story in an English lesson.

### Applying Bloom's Taxonomy to Classroom Objectives

When designing lessons, educators can integrate verbs associated with Bloom’s Taxonomy levels to ensure a range of cognitive tasks. For example, an elementary English Language Arts objective might start with students being able to *identify* the main idea (Remember), followed by summarizing key events (Understand), and eventually using context clues to interpret new vocabulary (Apply).

### Writing Objectives for Higher-Order Thinking

As students progress, teachers should build lessons that challenge them to move towards higher-order thinking. For example, in a middle school science class, students might begin by explaining the concept of the scientific method (Understand) but ultimately analyze real-world case studies and evaluate their findings (Evaluate).

These steps ensure that students are not only grasping content but also developing the ability to think critically and solve complex problems, which is the end goal of education.

### Preparing for Certification Exams Using Bloom’s Taxonomy

For those studying for teacher certification exams, understanding Bloom's Taxonomy is key to answering questions correctly, especially when test questions require identifying objectives that promote critical thinking. Look for verbs like *evaluate*, *analyze*, and *design* in both the test questions and the classroom activities they describe, as these typically indicate higher-order thinking skills.

To wrap it up, Bloom's Taxonomy is a powerful tool in guiding lesson planning and promoting student success. By steadily moving students through its levels, educators can ensure deeper understanding and foster critical thinking skills that will serve students well beyond the classroom.

args.summary:
Bloom's Taxonomy is a framework for categorizing educational goals, created by Benjamin Bloom in 1956. It helps teachers structure lessons and assessments to encourage higher levels of thinking. The taxonomy has six levels, from simplest to most complex: Remembering, Understanding, Applying, Analyzing, Evaluating, and Creating.

- **Remembering (Level 1):** Recalling facts and basic concepts (e.g., listing events, reciting formulas). Focuses on memorization and retention.
- **Understanding (Level 2):** Explaining ideas or concepts in one's own words (e.g., summarizing a chapter, explaining a process). Moves beyond memorization to grasp meaning.
- **Applying (Level 3):** Using information in new situations (e.g., solving unfamiliar problems with a formula, applying principles to real-world scenarios).
- **Analyzing (Level 4):** Breaking information into parts to understand relationships (e.g., comparing/contrasting theories, examining character motives).
- **Evaluating (Level 5):** Making judgments based on criteria and standards (e.g., critiquing writing, assessing argument validity). Requires critical thinking and justification.
- **Creating (Level 6):** Producing new or original work (e.g., writing a story, designing an experiment, developing novel solutions). Combines elements in unique ways.

**Criticism:** The taxonomy implies a strict, linear order of thinking skills, suggesting simpler skills must be mastered before complex ones. Critics argue learning is not this linear—people may analyze and create first to remember information, making the model overly simplistic and not reflective of real learning processes.

## Center for the Advancement of Teaching Excellence

# Bloom’s Taxonomy of Educational Objectives

## Introduction

Erin Stapleton-Corcoran*, CATE Instructional Designer*  
January 25, 2023

## WHAT?

### 1

**Bloom’s taxonomy is a hierarchical model used for classifying learning objectives by levels of complexity and specificity.** Bloom’s Taxonomy was created to outline and clarify how learners acquire new knowledge and skills. Though the original intention of the taxonomy was to serve as an assessment tool, Bloom’s taxonomy is effective in helping instructors identify clear learning objectives as well as create purposeful learning activities and instructional materials.

Bloom’s taxonomy emerged from a 1948 meeting of university educators – chaired by Benjamin Bloom – who brainstormed a theoretical model of learning that identified educational objectives to aid in the creation of testing items. The committee later expanded its initial framework to three learning domains:

### 2

![Illustration of a person holding three overlapping circles labeled cognitive, psychomotor, and affective against a purple background.](https://teaching.uic.edu/wp-content/uploads/sites/683/2023/03/Blooms-taxonomy.jpg)

Bloom’s Taxonomy consists of three learning domains: cognitive, affective and psychomotor.

## Cognitive Domain

### Cognitive Domain

### 1

The cognitive domain went through numerous revisions before a finalized version was published (Bloom 1956).

The cognitive domain has been the primary focus in education and has become shorthand for Bloom’s Taxonomy as a result. The cognitive domain is made up of six levels of objectives. These levels are organized by hierarchy, moving from foundational skills to higher-order thinking skills.

In 2001 Anderson and Krathwohl revised Bloom’s levels from nouns to verbs, and this is the version of the taxonomy used today.

### 2

![A pyramid diagram displaying six levels of Blooms taxonomy from bottom to top: Remember, Understand, Apply, Analyze, Evaluate, and Create. Each level is color-coded and labeled with bold text.](https://teaching.uic.edu/wp-content/uploads/sites/683/2023/03/TAX-pyramidCREATE.png)

*Anderson and Krathwohl revised Bloom’s levels from nouns to verbs.*

### 3

![A colorful 3D chart illustrating Anderson and Krathwohl’s two-dimensional taxonomy, mapping the Knowledge Dimension (factual, conceptual, procedural, metacognitive) against the Cognitive Process Dimension (remember, understand, apply, analyze, evaluate, create).](https://teaching.uic.edu/wp-content/uploads/sites/683/2023/03/2Dtaxonomy.png)

*Anderson and Krathwohl’s Two-Dimensional Taxonomy*

### 4

When revising Bloom’s Taxonomy in 2001, Anderson and Krathwohl also added the knowledge dimension to the taxonomy. The knowledge dimension consists of four dimensions, which are:

Based on this two-dimensional taxonomy, Anderson and Krathwohl developed a matrix for combining cognitive processes and knowledge dimensions which is shown to the left.

See the “[How](https://teaching.uic.edu/blooms-taxonomy-of-educational-objectives/#how)” section of this teaching guide to learn more about using the cognitive domain to craft learning objectives, assessments, and instructional materials and learning activities for your courses as well as how to implement the cognitive domain/knowledge dimension matrix when using Bloom’s Taxonomy in the classroom.

## Affective Domain

### Affective Domain

### 1

The affective domain was first published in 1964 (Krathwohl et al, 1964). The affective domain outlines skills and behaviors that correspond to attitudes and values and as the learner progresses through the levels of the affective domain, they become self-reliant and internally motivated.  Learning objectives aligned to the affective domain tend to be the hardest to articulate initially and often appear difficult to assess at first glance. However, affective outcomes often represent the outcomes most closely related to deeper thinking and lifelong learning.

The affective domain contains five levels, from lowest to highest:

See the “[How](https://teaching.uic.edu/resources/teaching-guides/learning-principles-and-frameworks/blooms-taxonomy-of-educational-objectives/#how)”  section of this teaching guide to learn more about using the affective domain to craft learning objectives, assessments, and instructional materials and learning activities for your courses.

### 2

![The five levels of the affective domain, from lowest to highest: receiving, responding, valuing, organizing, and characterizing.](https://teaching.uic.edu/wp-content/uploads/sites/683/2023/03/TAX-triangle-CHARACTERIZE.png)

*(Krathwohl et al., 1964)*

## Psychomotor Domain

### Psychomotor Domain

### 1

Bloom and his colleagues did not create subcategories for skills in the psychomotor domain, but other educators did (Simpson 1966, 1972;  Dave, 1970; Harrow, 1972). The psychomotor domain includes physical movement, coordination, and motor skills. Development of these skills requires practice and is measured in terms of speed, precision, distance, procedures, or technical execution. For the purpose of this teaching guide, we will explore Simpson’s version of the psychomotor domain, which has the following seven levels:

### 2

![Simpson’s seven levels of the psychomotor domain, from lowest to highest: perception, set, guided response, mechanism, complex overt response, adaptation, and origination.](https://teaching.uic.edu/wp-content/uploads/sites/683/2023/03/TAX-triangle-ORIGINATION.png)

*Simpson’s seven levels of the psychomotor domain.*

See the “[How](https://teaching.uic.edu/blooms-taxonomy-of-educational-objectives/#how)” section of this teaching guide to learn more about using the psychomotor domain to craft learning objectives, assessments, and instructional materials and learning activities for your courses.

## WHY?

### There are several benefits to applying Bloom’s taxonomy to your teaching.

### 1

### 2

## HOW?

### How can you use Bloom’s Taxonomy to craft learning objectives?

### 1

Bloom’s Taxonomy can help you write clear [learning objectives](https://teaching.uic.edu/learning-objectives/), which are a description of what the learner must be able to do upon completion of an educational activity. A well-written learning objective outlines the knowledge, skills, and/or attitude the learners will gain from the educational activity and does so in an observable and measurable way.

More specifically, Bloom’s can help you identify the level, criteria, or standards for the knowledge, skills, abilities, competencies, attitudes, or values that your students are expected to be able to demonstrate.

For the cognitive, affective, and psychomotor domains, there are action verbs that align with each level. These action verbs are invaluable in crafting effective learning objectives.

### 2

Use the following steps to craft learning objectives using Bloom’s taxonomy:

Consult the tables below to view action verbs that align with each level of the cognitive, affective, and psychomotor domains, as well as examples for each of the levels.

## Cognitive domain

**Cognitive domain**

This domain is focused on intellectual skills such as critical thinking, problem-solving, and creating a knowledge base. The cognitive hierarchy consists of six levels, which span from simple memorization designed to build the knowledge of learners, to creating something new based on previously-learned information.

## How can you use Bloom’s Taxonomy in the classroom?

**How can you use Bloom’s Taxonomy in the classroom?**  
There are many ways that Bloom’s can be applied to course planning to ensure effective instruction and student learning is occurring.  Several approaches to lesson planning that build on Bloom’s Taxonomy are described below.

### Expertise pathways

### Expertise pathways

Expertise pathways involve using increasingly sophisticated cognitive processes to accumulate deeper understanding. This deeper understanding or expertise can be accomplished by moving through Bloom’s levels to explore a discrete learning topic or concept. The example below demonstrates expertise in the cognitive domain, focusing on a particular play script (Gershon 2013).

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| Remember the names and relationships of a cast of characters in a play | A multiple-choice test designed to test the memory of learners. |
| Explain the main ideas of a play | Write a short (1 page) paper summarizing the plot and most important events in the play. |
| Apply the main ideas/themes in the play to another context | Write an advice column responding to one of the characters. |
| Analyze the roles of each character in the play and their relationships to each other. | Write an analytical paper comparing the antagonists and protagonists of the play. |
| Evaluate the decisions of characters in the play, and support your evaluation with textual evidence. | Write a response to one of the events in the play, either supporting or rejecting their actions on the basis of evidence from the play as well as personal opinion and projected/actual consequences of action. |
| Create a new and unique piece of writing using similar plot devices. | Create a short story using similar plot devices in a new time or setting. |

## Three-part lesson

### Three-part lesson

### Three-part lesson

### 1

Another technique Gershon suggests is to divide the taxonomy into sections. For example, he splits the levels of the cognitive domain into three sections:  remember and understand, apply and analyze, and evaluate and create. Then, he divides the lesson into three segments and focuses on one of the three sections of the domains in that lesson segment.

To implement Gershon’s technique, divide your lesson into three segments. Assign “remember and understand” to the first segment, “apply and analyze” to the second segment,  and “evaluate and create” to the third segment of the lesson.

Alternatively, Crowe et al (2008) divide Bloom’s taxonomy into two sections referred to as lower order cognitive skills (LOCS) and higher order cognitive skills (HOCS) to better align  assessments with learning activities in college-level Biology classes.  LOCS comprise the first three cognitive levels of Bloom’s Taxonomy (remember, understand, and apply) whereas HOCS include the second three levels (analyze, evaluate, and create).

## Teach with Anderson and Krathwohl’s Two Dimension Taxonomy: Cognitive Processes and Knowledge Dimensions

### Teach with Anderson and Krathwohl’s Two Dimension Taxonomy: Cognitive Processes and Knowledge Dimensions

### Teach with Anderson and Krathwohl’s Two Dimension Taxonomy: Cognitive Processes and Knowledge Dimensions

Another way to enhance the use of Bloom’s Taxonomy is by considering learning objectives simultaneously through Anderson and Krathwohl’s Two Dimensional Taxonomy: Cognitive Processes and Knowledge Dimensions Matrix. Richlin (2006) adapted this matrix for planning courses and lessons, which is shown in the table below. Examples of learning objectives that intersect the cognitive process and knowledge dimension are also detailed.

| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |

|  | Factual Knowledge: basic elements to learn or solve problems in the discipline | Remember + Factual List primary and secondary colors | Understand + Factual Summarize features of a new product | Apply + Factual Respond to frequently asked questions | Analyze + Factual Select the most complete list of activities | Evaluate + Factual Check for consistency among sources | Create + Factual Generate a log of daily activities |

|  | Metacognitive Knowledge: awareness of how learning work in relation to one’s self | Remember + Metacognitive Identify strategies for retaining information | Understand + Metacognitive Predict one’s response to culture shock | Apply + Metacognitive Use techniques that match one's strengths | Analyze + Metacognitive Deconstruct one's biases | Evaluate + Metacognitive Reflect on one's progress | Create + Metacognitive Create a learning portfolio |

args.summary:
This webpage from the University of Illinois Chicago's Center for the Advancement of Teaching Excellence (CATE), authored by Erin Stapleton-Corcoran on January 25, 2023, provides a comprehensive guide to Bloom's Taxonomy of Educational Objectives.

**What is Bloom's Taxonomy?**
Bloom's taxonomy is a hierarchical model for classifying learning objectives by levels of complexity and specificity. It originated from a 1948 meeting chaired by Benjamin Bloom and consists of three learning domains: cognitive, affective, and psychomotor.

**Cognitive Domain (Primary Focus)**
- Published in 1956 (Bloom), revised in 2001 by Anderson and Krathwohl who changed levels from nouns to verbs and added a knowledge dimension.
- Six levels (lowest to highest): Remember, Understand, Apply, Analyze, Evaluate, Create.
- The knowledge dimension has four types: Factual, Conceptual, Procedural, and Metacognitive Knowledge.
- The revised taxonomy creates a two-dimensional matrix combining cognitive processes with knowledge dimensions.

**Affective Domain (Krathwohl et al., 1964)**
- Focuses on attitudes, values, and interests.
- Five levels: Receiving, Responding, Valuing, Organizing, Characterizing.

**Psychomotor Domain**
- Developed by other educators (Simpson 1966, 1972; Dave, 1970; Harrow, 1972).
- Simpson's version has seven levels: Perception, Set, Guided Response, Mechanism, Complex Overt Response, Adaptation, Origination.

**How to Use Bloom's Taxonomy**
The guide provides extensive tables of action verbs for each level across all three domains, along with example learning objectives. It includes sample objectives across disciplines (linguistics, biology, English/literature, public health, engineering).

**Classroom Applications**
1. Expertise pathways - moving through Bloom's levels to explore a topic
2. Differentiated instruction (all/most/some outcomes)
3. Three-part lesson - dividing taxonomy into sections (remember/understand, apply/analyze, evaluate/create)
4. Two-dimensional taxonomy matrix for course planning

The guide also discusses lower-order cognitive skills (LOCS: remember, understand, apply) vs. higher-order cognitive skills (HOCS: analyze, evaluate, create).
